title: Reinforcement Learning Control for a Wave Energy Converter
kicker: Graduate Project · Oregon State University · Energy Systems
tools: Python · Gymnasium · WEC-Sim (Wave Energy Converter Simulator) · MATLAB / Simulink · Stable-Baselines3 PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) · OSU HPC (Oregon State University high-performance computing) · W&B (Weights & Biases)
blurb: A Python interface that lets RL (reinforcement learning) agents step a full WEC-Sim wave simulation; a PPO agent trained on a cheap linear model transferred with no loss.
long: A wave energy converter (WEC) turns ocean wave motion into electricity, and the force its generator applies at each moment decides how much energy it harvests. RL (reinforcement learning) could learn that force directly, but the standard simulator, WEC-Sim, runs in MATLAB and Simulink with no Python control loop.

The interface. wecsim_gym wraps WEC-Sim as a Gymnasium environment: the action is the force, the reward is energy absorbed. It matches a Simulink-only reference to about 1e-10 in mean power, and five RL libraries train on it unchanged.

Cheap model versus full simulator. A PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) agent trained on the group's linear model reached 148.8 kW in WEC-Sim, level with the best tuned damper (147.4 kW), and trained in 2.4 minutes instead of 71. The next step is training across many sea states, where a fixed damper cannot keep up.
highlights: Gymnasium interface matches a Simulink-only reference to ~1e-10 in mean power
19.9 ms per 0.1 s control step on an HPC (high-performance computing) node; 5 RL (reinforcement learning) libraries train unchanged
PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) trained on a linear model: 148.8 kW on WEC-Sim vs 147.4 kW tuned damper, in 2.4 min instead of 71
Linear model vs WEC-Sim motion correlation ≥ 0.9985 across three wave seeds
